name: hash-wasm
language: C compiled to WebAssembly, TypeScript wrapper
baseline: Pure JavaScript and other WASM hash libraries from npm: spark-md5, md5-wasm, crypto-js, node-forge, jsSHA, noble-hashes, sha256-wasm, sha3-wasm, xxhashjs, xxhash-wasm, argon2-browser
workload: Hash throughput for 32-byte and 1 MB inputs (MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA3-512, XXHash64) plus PBKDF2-SHA512 (1000 iterations) and Argon2id (m=512, t=8, p=1) operations per second, measured in Chrome v131.
claimed_speedup: 1 MB inputs: MD5 850.31 MB/s vs spark-md5 171.73 MB/s and crypto-js 46.71 MB/s; SHA1 798.19 MB/s vs jsSHA 78.12 MB/s; SHA256 426.16 MB/s vs noble-hashes 110.02 MB/s, sha256-wasm 308.39 MB/s and crypto-js 65.17 MB/s; SHA3-512 234.40 MB/s vs noble-hashes 14.19 MB/s; XXHash64 15,989 MB/s vs xxhash-wasm 15,929 MB/s (a tie) and xxhashjs 42.26 MB/s. PBKDF2-SHA512: 588 ops/s vs noble-hashes 395 and crypto-js 29. Argon2id: 438 ops/s vs argon2-browser 213.
hardware: Ryzen 9 7900X desktop CPU, Chrome v131 (stated in the README footnote)
tradeoffs: Promise-based async API, one WASM binary per algorithm, needs WebAssembly (README support table: Chrome 57+, Safari 11+, Firefox 53+, Edge 16+, Node.js 8+, Deno 1+, IE not supported). The README lists WebAssembly SIMD under future plans (expected 10-20% gain), so the numbers are scalar WASM. No native crypto fallback.
caveats: First-party README tables; the README shows hash-wasm 4.10.0 while the latest release found was 4.12.0. Compiler version and flags are not stated and the browser benchmark page (daninet.github.io, linked from the README) was not opened. The README never compares against Node's built-in crypto (OpenSSL) or WebCrypto, so the baseline is only JavaScript or other WASM packages. Small-input (32 byte) numbers are dominated by call overhead. XXHash64 on 1 MB ties with xxhash-wasm.
found_via: WebSearch (npmjs.com results) 'WebAssembly "faster than" pure JavaScript implementation npm package benchmark wasm-powered library "x faster"' surfaced hash-wasm; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com and repo page via github.com

name: xxhash-wasm
language: WebAssembly with JavaScript wrapper (implementation of xxHash 32-bit and 64-bit)
baseline: xxhashjs (pure JavaScript xxHash, uses cuint for 64-bit math); also Node built-in crypto md5 and sha1 (different, cryptographic algorithms)
workload: ops/sec hashing random strings from 1 byte to 100,000,000 bytes with Benchmark.js, instance creation excluded.
claimed_speedup: README: 32-bit up to 90x and 64-bit up to 350x faster than xxhashjs. Examples: 1,000,000 bytes xxhashjs 32-bit 36.40 ops/s and 64-bit 12.93 ops/s vs xxhash-wasm 32-bit 5,122 ops/s and 64-bit 8,632 ops/s; 100 bytes xxhashjs 32-bit 425,277 ops/s vs xxhash-wasm 32-bit 5,470,011 ops/s. Against Node crypto at 1,000,000 bytes: md5 698 ops/s and sha1 966 ops/s vs xxhash-wasm 64-bit 8,632 ops/s.
hardware: Not stated for the xxhashjs table; the Node crypto comparison table says an x64 MacBook Pro running Node 17.3
tradeoffs: Needs BigInt in WASM, bulk memory and TextEncoder.encodeInto (Chrome >= 85, Firefox >= 79, Safari >= 15, Node >= 15); older xxhash-wasm 0.4.2 is 3-4x slower. WASM instantiation takes about 1 ms in the browser and a little over 2 ms in Node. Small bundle (11.4 kB minified, 2.3 kB gzipped) versus xxhashjs 41.5 kB.
caveats: First-party README numbers with the hardware missing for the main table; it compares only against a slow pure-JS library that emulates 64-bit integers, not against a native xxHash binding or the C reference (the xxHash C library is already catalogued). Node crypto rows compare a non-cryptographic hash against md5/sha1, which is not like for like. A WebSearch snippet of an older npm page quoted 11x and 74x, so the README numbers have changed between versions. A SIMD port attempt in issue #29 was reported as not promising.
found_via: WebSearch 'WebAssembly SIMD port benchmark "faster than native" OR "near-native" OR "outperforms JavaScript" library github hash codec' (result: jungomi/xxhash-wasm issue #29); README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: TensorFlow.js WASM backend (tfjs-backend-wasm)
language: C++ (XNNPACK) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten via Bazel, TypeScript wrapper
baseline: TensorFlow.js plain JS (CPU) backend; WebGL backend also shown
workload: Inference time for MobileNet V2 (3.48M params, ~300M multiply-adds) and a Face Detector model (0.1M params, ~20M multiply-adds), averaged over 200 runs in Chrome 79.0 on phones and desktops.
claimed_speedup: README: MobileNet V2 WASM is about 3X-11.5X faster than the plain JS backend (MacBook Pro 15 2019: 98.4 ms WASM, 893.5 ms plain JS, 30.2 ms WASM+SIMD, 10.3 ms WASM+SIMD+threads; ThinkPad X1 Gen6: 122.7 ms vs 1489.4 ms plain JS) and 5.3-7.7X slower than WebGL. Face Detector WASM is about 8.2-19.8X faster than plain JS and comparable to WebGL (Desktop Linux: 12.6 ms vs 249.5 ms plain JS; 8.0 ms with SIMD; 6.2 ms with SIMD and threads). The FAQ says WASM is strictly faster than plain JS on all devices and model sizes.
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten through the Bazel Emscripten toolchain; optimisation flags not stated in the README
hardware: iPhone X, iPhone XS, Pixel 4, ThinkPad X1 Gen6 (Linux), Desktop Windows, Desktop Linux, MacBook Pro 15 2019, Node v14 on a MacBook Pro; Chrome 79.0; CPU models not stated
tradeoffs: Beats the pure-JS CPU backend but is several times slower than WebGL on medium models; SIMD and multithreaded variants ship as separate .wasm binaries (threads need cross-origin isolation); the README says WASM has better numerical stability and wider device support than WebGL.
caveats: First-party numbers from Chrome 79 (early 2020), when WASM SIMD and threads were still experimental, so the absolute figures are old. The baseline is TensorFlow.js's own JS kernels, not another optimised JS tensor library and not the native TensorFlow build. Last commit date is for the whole monorepo, not the backend directory. Compiler flags and CPU models are missing. The XNNPACK library itself (google/xnnpack) is already catalogued.
found_via: github.com/topics/wasm?l=typescript&s=stars listed tensorflow/tfjs; tfjs-backend-wasm README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: markdown-wasm
language: C (md4c) compiled to WebAssembly, JavaScript API
baseline: markdown-it, marked, commonmark and showdown (pure JavaScript Markdown parsers)
workload: Parse markdown and render HTML for a set of sample files in test/benchmark, average ops/second across the samples, one CPU thread, NodeJS v14.11.0.
claimed_speedup: Average ops/second from the README graph (avg-ops-per-sec.svg): markdown-wasm 195,065; markdown-it 84,774; marked 76,942; commonmark 66,185; showdown 8,502 (about 2.3x markdown-it and 2.5x marked, derived from page data).
hardware: 2.9 GHz MacBook running macOS 10.15, NodeJS v14.11.0 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Zero dependencies, 31 kB gzipped; CommonMark compliant through md4c; WASM runs in isolated memory; the API docs warn that the onCodeBlock callback hurts performance because it bridges WASM and JS on every block; output is HTML only, and returning bytes (bytes=true) only helps when the output is never converted to a string.
caveats: First-party; the benchmark results are SVG images and the numbers above were read from the SVG text, not from a table. Old Node 14 numbers, no CPU model, compiler flags not examined, library versions of the JS competitors not stated. It is a wrapper around md4c (mity/md4c is already catalogued), so it may fold into that entry as a duplicate. No comparison against native md4c.

name: wasmoon
language: C (official Lua 5.4) compiled to WebAssembly, TypeScript bindings
workload: Heap sort (bench/heapsort.lua) of a list of 2k numbers, run 10 times, from the README comparison table.
claimed_speedup: README: wasmoon 15.267 ms vs fengari 389.923 ms (about 25x, derived from page data); README text says wasmoon runs Lua much faster than Fengari unless there is a lot of JS to Lua interop.
tradeoffs: Larger bundle than Fengari (393 kB plain and 130 kB gzipped vs 214 kB and 69 kB); JS-to-Lua interop is expensive and can erase the gain; needs WebAssembly; wraps the real Lua 5.4 so semantics match PUC Lua rather than Fengari's Lua 5.3.
caveats: One micro-benchmark with no hardware, browser or Node version, and the '10x (less is better)' wording does not say whether times are per run or for the ten runs. First-party. Lua itself (lua/lua) is already catalogued and no comparison against native Lua is given.
found_via: Direct fetch of the project README (recalled as a WASM Lua port while reviewing JS-versus-WASM interpreters); no search query surfaced it; repo page and commit feed read via github.com

name: DuckDB-Wasm
language: C++ (DuckDB) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten, TypeScript API
baseline: Arquero (JavaScript dataframe library) and SQLite WASM; danfo also in the table
workload: Third-party in-browser benchmark on 1,000,000 Bandcamp sales rows (24 columns): analytical SELECTs (overall metrics, group by day, top 5 countries per item and slug type, random rows) plus index, update, insert and delete tests, run on a separate browser thread.
claimed_speedup: Intel i7-1165G7 + Chrome 116 (times as printed, unit not labelled in the table, likely seconds): Test 1 overall metrics duckdb 0.014 vs arquero 0.067 and sqlite 0.376; Test 3 top 5 countries duckdb 0.114 vs arquero 4.847 and sqlite 1.432 (about 42x Arquero, derived from page data); Test 4 random rows duckdb 0.032 vs arquero 0.517. Apple M2 + Firefox 117: Test 3 duckdb 0.132 vs arquero 0.852 and sqlite 1.025. Not a clean win: indexed SQLite WASM is faster on group-by-day (0.005 vs 0.163) and on transactional tests 6-9 (sqlite 0.054, 0.038, 0.041, 0.035 vs duckdb 1.048, 0.588, 1.397, 2.376).
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 @2.80GHz Windows laptop with Chrome 116; Apple M2 MacBook Air with Firefox 117
tradeoffs: Large WASM download; extensions such as Parquet, JSON and ICU are autoloaded lazily; HTTP stack differs from native DuckDB (CORS and HTTPS required); weaker than SQLite WASM on small transactional updates.
caveats: The independent benchmark is a small hobbyist repo (7 stars) measured in 2023-era browsers; the DuckDB-Wasm version, WASM build flags and units are not stated, and fetch/load rows depend on network and cache. B rather than A because the build compiler and flags are missing. DuckDB-Wasm's own VLDB 2022 paper and the shell.duckdb.org/versus TPC-H page (against sql.js, Arquero, Lovefield) could not be opened (host blocked), and WebSearch snippets give no numbers. Native DuckDB is not compared; duckdb/duckdb is already catalogued.

name: gmp-wasm
language: C (GMP and MPFR) compiled to WebAssembly, TypeScript wrapper
baseline: JavaScript built-in BigInt (also big-integer and decimal.js)
workload: Computing 8000 digits of Pi with a series formula (benchmark/calcpi.js), average time, Node.js v16.14.
claimed_speedup: BigInt 129 ms; gmp-wasm Integer() wrapper 88 ms (1.47x), with delayed deallocation 78 ms (1.65x), low-level MPZ 53 ms (2.43x); big-integer 129 ms (1x); decimal.js 443 ms (0.29x). Floats: Float() wrapper 175 ms (0.74x, slower than BigInt), MPFR low-level 118 ms (1.09x). Float(1).atan().mul(4) 0.6 ms (215x) and Float('0.5').asin().mul(6) 17 ms (7.59x).
hardware: Intel Kaby Lake desktop CPU (model not stated), Node.js v16.14
tradeoffs: LGPL-3.0 (GMP/MPFR); manual memory management through binding.reset() and a lower-level MPZ/MPFR API is needed for the best numbers; WASM size and init cost; adds rationals and floats that BigInt lacks.
caveats: One workload with the author's own harness; the headline gains need the low-level API and the high-level Float wrapper is slower than BigInt; Node 16 BigInt is older than current V8. The 215x and 7.59x rows are transcendental-function rows (atan, asin) and the README does not say what the baseline for those two rows is. A wasm port of GMP and MPFR, which are already catalogued (gmplib.org, mpfr.org); native GMP speed is not compared.
found_via: Direct fetch of the README after reading hash-wasm (same author); no search query surfaced it; repo page and commit feed read via github.com

name: iswasmfast
language: C++ compiled to WebAssembly and to an N-API addon, JavaScript harness
baseline: Pure JavaScript implementation (labelled 'Native' in the README) and the same C++ code built as a Node.js N-API addon
workload: Levenshtein distance, Fibonacci, Fermat primality test, simple linear regression and SHA256 in Node.js, benchmark.js ops/sec.
claimed_speedup: Fibonacci: WebAssembly 11,508,910 ops/s vs N-API addon 5,204,691 and JS 4,044,156. Fermat primality: WebAssembly 2,402,964 vs addon 1,833,692 and JS 1,678,845. SHA256: addon 67,807, WebAssembly 34,445, JS 13,453. WebAssembly loses on Levenshtein (210,776 vs addon 308,924 and JS 295,433) and on simple linear regression (WebAssembly 37,117 and 42,521 with TypedArrays vs JS 291,985).
tradeoffs: Mixed result by design: WASM beats the same C++ built as an addon when per-call overhead dominates (Fibonacci, Fermat) but loses where data is copied across the boundary (regression, Levenshtein).
caveats: Toy kernels with +-9-15% reported variance; no CPU, Node version, compiler or flags stated, and the README labels the JS version 'Native'. Included because it directly measures WASM against the same code compiled natively as an addon, but WASM wins on only two of five tasks. Medium blog post referenced is not opened.
found_via: WebSearch '"compiled to WebAssembly" "times faster than" JavaScript library benchmark README' (github.com results) listed zandaqo/iswasmfast; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: BenchmarkingWebAssembly (Understanding the Performance of WebAssembly Applications)
language: C (PolyBenchC and CHStone) compiled by Cheerp to WebAssembly and JavaScript; Python test scripts
baseline: JavaScript produced from the same C programs by Cheerp 2.0
workload: 41 PolyBenchC and CHStone benchmarks plus other subjects at extra-small, small and medium input sizes, WASM vs JS execution time in Chrome 79, Firefox 71 and Edge 79, desktop and mobile.
claimed_speedup: README: with extra-small and small inputs WebAssembly is faster than JavaScript in almost all benchmarks (97.6% and 95.1%), with average speedups of 26.99x (extra-small) and 8.22x (small); with medium inputs 18 benchmarks become slower in WebAssembly (average slowdown 1.71x). Example: 3mm is 47.71x, 10.54x and 1.12x faster in WebAssembly for extra-small, small and medium inputs.
compiler_and_flags: Cheerp 2.0, tested at -O1, -O2, -Ofast and -Oz (README); Chrome 79, Firefox 71, Edge 79
tradeoffs: A study, not a library: the JS baseline is machine-generated by Cheerp rather than idiomatic hand-written JavaScript, and WASM's advantage shrinks or reverses as input grows; repo has no license, so the code is reference only.
caveats: The README is the abstract of a paper but names no venue, year or link on the opened pages, so peer review could not be confirmed and the tier is capped at C (a retier to B is possible once the paper is reachable). Hardware is not stated in the README; browsers are from 2019-2020. Raw data is in test_results. Mixed outcome rather than a pure win.
found_via: WebSearch '"compiled to WebAssembly" "times faster than" JavaScript library benchmark README' (github.com results) listed BenchmarkingWasm/BenchmarkingWebAssembly

name: tiny-secp256k1 (WASM build)
language: Rust (wrapping the C libsecp256k1) compiled to WebAssembly, TypeScript wrapper
baseline: elliptic (pure JavaScript, the fallback of tiny-secp256k1 1.1.6); the Rust native addon is faster than the WASM build
workload: ECDSA sign and verify micro-benchmarks from the repo's benches directory, posted by the maintainer in PR #53 (March 2021).
claimed_speedup: Intel i5-8250U Linux: sign WASM 469.03 us/op (2132.07 op/s) vs elliptic 913.58 us/op (1094.60 op/s); verify WASM 605.01 us/op (1652.87 op/s) vs elliptic 2576.87 us/op (388.07 op/s). Apple M1: sign WASM 133.19 us/op vs elliptic 522.64 us/op; verify WASM 212.05 us/op vs elliptic 1515.26 us/op. Author summary: 'Wasm vs js: 2x for sign and pk creation, 4x for verify'. The Rust addon did sign in 51.71 us/op (19340.42 op/s), about 9x faster than WASM on that machine (derived from page data). README: the wasm2js asm.js build is 10x-20x slower than WASM and noble-based @bitcoinerlab/secp256k1 is 1.5x-5x slower than WASM.
compiler_and_flags: Rust >= 1.50.0 with wasm32-unknown-unknown and wasm-opt from binaryen (README build section); flags not stated
hardware: Intel i5-8250U (Linux); Apple M1; a Debian i686 VirtualBox run without an elliptic row; Node.js version not stated
tradeoffs: One portable WASM binary replaces the old C++ addon plus elliptic fallback; slower than node native bindings, so on Node the native addon would be the faster choice; JS BigInt alternatives are 1.5x-5x slower than this WASM per the README.
caveats: The benchmark is a maintainer comment from 2021, not a documented suite, and the README itself only says WASM is 'faster than elliptic but slower than node bindings'. The compiler flags and Node version are not stated. libsecp256k1 (bitcoin-core/secp256k1) is already catalogued.

name: Pare
language: C (x264, SVT-AV1, libvmaf) compiled to WebAssembly SIMD128 with Emscripten, TypeScript web app
baseline: ffmpeg.wasm 0.12 (x264 built without its assembly) single-threaded and multithreaded; native x264 as the ceiling
workload: Compress Big Buck Bunny (10 s, 30.7 MB) to at least 50% smaller at matching VMAF NEG in headless Chrome, including the size plan and test encodes, on a 4-core 8-thread cloud VM.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md: Pare 24.9 s (13.4 MB, VMAF NEG 93.1) vs ffmpeg.wasm 0.12 one thread 158.9 s (6.4x slower) and multithreaded 42.4 s (1.7x slower) at about the same VMAF NEG; native ffmpeg x264 6.4 s; Pare's encode alone 12.9 s, twice native x264 on the same cores. README: about 1,500 lines of WebAssembly SIMD128 kernels (SAD, SATD, interpolation, DCT, quantization, deblocking) make encoding 2.0-2.3x faster per core and run at 54% of native x264 with the same settings; whole encodes are byte-identical to the plain C build.
compiler_and_flags: emcc with -O3 -msimd128 (x264-wasm/build.sh); Emscripten and Chrome versions not pinned
hardware: Xeon Platinum 8259CL 2.5 GHz (2019), 4 cores / 8 threads cloud VM shared with other work, no GPU
tradeoffs: GPL because of x264; needs WebAssembly SIMD128 and Web Workers; chunked parallel encoding costs 4-9% more bytes than a single encode; the app picks its own rate factor to hit a size target;
caveats: First-party and a very new project (94 commits, first in late September 2026); part of the speedup over ffmpeg.wasm comes from chunked multi-worker encoding and WebCodecs decoding, not only the SIMD kernels, and the ffmpeg.wasm rows were given a fixed CRF while Pare's time includes finding its own. Reproducible from public scripts (research/benchmark.mjs, score.py) but the machine was shared with other work and one clip is shown per row. Tier A is borderline because the Emscripten and Chrome versions are not stated. ffmpeg/ffmpeg is already catalogued; x264 itself was not found in the known list.
found_via: github.com/topics/wasm-simd listed x1xhlol/pare; README and research/BENCHMARKS.md read via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com

name: fast-pako (@r1ck404/fast-pako)
language: Rust compiled to WebAssembly (zlib port) with JavaScript wrapper
workload: ungzip, inflate and deflate calls on npm tarballs and JavaScript files from 75 bytes to 9 MB, best of 3 rounds in fresh processes, Node 24.16 (some rows also in Chromium 149).
claimed_speedup: ungzip typescript 5.9.3 npm tarball (4.4 MB) 99.8 ms vs 17.3 ms (5.8x); inflate 9 MB of JavaScript 28.1 ms vs 6.7 ms (4.2x); deflateRaw level 1 on 1 MB 9.9 ms vs 3.2 ms (3.0x); deflate level 6 on 1 MB 32.8 ms vs 15.7 ms (2.1x); level 9 140.2 ms vs 64.3 ms (2.2x); deflate level 6 on 75 B 80.6 us vs 4.0 us (20x); import plus first ungzip of a 1.4 MB tarball 49.7 ms vs 12.2 ms.
tradeoffs: Drop-in for pako 2.1.0 with byte-identical output and TypeScript types; throws if WebAssembly is unavailable; the WASM is embedded and loads synchronously on first use; deflate at levels 6 and 9 gains only about 2x because the zlib match finder must stay identical.
caveats: First-party numbers on a repository that is only days old (first commit 2026-09-27) with 1 star; best of 3 rounds, raw data is in the repo's results directory. The only baseline is pako; native Node zlib, zlib-ng or fflate are not compared, so it is a JS-equivalent win and not a win against native zlib. The repo covers several packages (fast-acorn, fast-esbuild-wasm, fast-es-module-lexer, fast-brotli-wasm, fast-noble-hashes), this entry is the zlib port only; the repo URL points at its package directory.

name: fast-noble-hashes (@r1ck404/fast-noble-hashes)
language: WebAssembly (SHA-2, SHA-1, MD5, PBKDF2 loop, scrypt ROMix) with JavaScript, drop-in for @noble/hashes
workload: One-shot and streaming hashes, HMAC, PBKDF2 and scrypt calls on npm tarballs and short strings, best of 3 rounds, Node 24.16 and headless Chromium.
claimed_speedup: sha512 on typescript 5.9.3 tarball (4.4 MB) 30.47 ms vs 5.68 ms (5.4x Node, 6.0x Chromium); sha256 1 MB 3.65 ms vs 2.12 ms (1.7x Node, 2.3x Chromium); sha1 1 MB 2.64 ms vs 1.01 ms (2.6x, 4.3x Chromium); md5 1 MB 8.95 ms vs 1.15 ms (7.8x); pbkdf2(sha512) c=10000 24.17 ms vs 3.36 ms (7.2x Node, 8.2x Chromium); scrypt N=2^14 36.32 ms vs 16.06 ms (2.3x).
tradeoffs: Needs WebAssembly with SIMD (accelerated functions throw without it); SHA-3, BLAKE, RIPEMD-160 and Argon2 run noble's unchanged code; a single sha256 or md5 import is larger than noble's.
caveats: The package page says Node's built-in crypto is used for large one-shot hashes when process.getBuiltinModule is available, so the Node column for big inputs may measure OpenSSL rather than the WASM; the Chromium column is WASM-only. First-party numbers on a days-old, 1-star repository, and baseline is only pure-JS noble (hash-wasm, native crypto and WebCrypto are not compared). The repo URL points at the package directory of R1ck404/fast-packages.
